title: Obligations V — Lex Aquilia and suretyship (class 16 Dec)

1.title: Delicts and the text of the LEX AQUILIA
1.text:
Lesson of 16 December 2026 (Obligations; Lex Aquilia / surety). Assessment II (13 January 2027) is an exegesis of a Digest fragment on the law of obligations. Page references: 'Obl.' = Benke/Meissel, Roman Law of Obligations; 'Prop.' = Benke/Meissel, Roman Law of Property.

### Where we are in the system
A duty to pay damages arises EX CONTRACTU (breach of a duty taken on by contract) or EX DELICTO (breach of a duty owed to everyone) (Obl. pp. 310–311). A loss stays where it falls, unless someone caused it UNLAWFULLY and CULPABLY (p. 309).

Two kinds of sanction (pp. 311–312):
- **Indemnification**: making good the loss, never more. Actions of this kind are REIPERSECUTORY.
- **Penalty (POENA)**: punishment and deterrence. In Rome the injured party himself sues for it and keeps the fine. Such actions are PENAL.

The delicts you meet: FURTUM (theft), INIURIA (insult and injury to a free Roman), DOLUS and METUS, and DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM ('loss unlawfully caused'), which the jurists built on the LEX AQUILIA (pp. 313–316).

### The statute (Obl. pp. 326–327)
The LEX AQUILIA (date uncertain, probably 3rd century BC) is the main Roman source on damage to property. Only chapters 1 and 3 matter.

**Chapter 1:** SI QUIS SERVUM SERVAMVE ALIENUM ALIENAMVE QUADRUPEDEMVE PECUDEM INIURIA OCCIDERIT, QUANTI ID IN EO ANNO PLURIMI FUIT, TANTUM AES DARE DOMINO DAMNAS ESTO. In short: whoever wrongfully kills another's slave or four-legged herd animal pays the OWNER the highest value it had in that year (cf Gaius D 9.2.2 pr).

**Chapter 3:** SI QUIS ALTERI DAMNUM FAXIT, QUOD USSERIT FREGERIT RUPERIT INIURIA, QUANTI EA RES ERIT IN DIEBUS TRIGINTA PROXIMIS, TANTUM AES DOMINO DARE DAMNAS ESTO. In short: whoever causes loss by wrongful burning, breaking or 'rending' pays the owner what the matter comes to within the next 30 days (cf Ulpian D 9.2.27.5).

The jurists' INTERPRETATIO turned these few words into a whole law of damages (p. 326, fn 1).

### An ACTIO MIXTA (pp. 316–317)
The ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE compensates, but has a minor penal element: the HIGHEST value of the past year can exceed the real loss; several wrongdoers each pay in full, because payment by one does not free the others, 'CUM SIT POENA' (Ulpian D 9.2.11.2); a defendant who denies the deed pays DOUBLE (Gai. 4.9; litiscrescence, p. 368).

terms.def: The delict of loss unlawfully caused: unlawful and culpable destruction of or damage to another's property, built by the jurists on the LEX AQUILIA (Obl. p. 316).
An action that is both reipersecutory and penal; the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE compensates the loss but has a minor penal element (Obl. pp. 316–317).

cards.q: What does chapter 1 of the LEX AQUILIA provide?
cards.a:
Whoever wrongfully (INIURIA) kills (OCCIDERE) another's slave or four-legged herd animal must pay the owner its HIGHEST value in that year.
• QUANTI ID IN EO ANNO PLURIMI FUIT … DOMINO DARE DAMNAS ESTO
• cf Gaius D 9.2.2 pr

cards.q: What does chapter 3 of the LEX AQUILIA provide?
cards.a:
Whoever causes loss to another by wrongful burning, breaking or 'rending' (URERE, FRANGERE, RUMPERE) must pay the owner what the matter comes to within the next 30 days.
• QUANTI EA RES ERIT IN DIEBUS TRIGINTA PROXIMIS
• cf Ulpian D 9.2.27.5

cards.q: Penal action vs reipersecutory action — what is the difference?
cards.a:
A reipersecutory action makes good the loss (never more); a penal action punishes and deters, and the fine goes to the injured party.
• Reipersecutory: CONDICTIO FURTIVA, REI VINDICATIO, contractual actions
• Penal: ACTIO FURTI, ACTIO INIURIARUM

cards.q: Why is the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE called an ACTIO MIXTA?
cards.a:
It compensates the loss but also has a minor penal element.
• Highest value of the past year can exceed the real loss
• Several wrongdoers each pay in full: 'CUM SIT POENA' (Ulpian D 9.2.11.2)
• A defendant who denies the deed pays double (Gai. 4.9)

2.title: Property law you need here
2.text:
The LEX AQUILIA protects PROPERTY, so 'who sues whom?' is a property-law question.

### The owner is the claimant
DOMINIUM is the right that gives the owner (DOMINUS) exclusive control over a thing (Prop. p. 68). The statute says DOMINO DARE: the owner is primarily entitled to sue (Ulpian D 9.2.11.6, Obl. p. 365). A slave is a thing, so for a killed or injured slave the MASTER sues for his financial loss, not for the slave's pain (Obl. p. 321). Co-owners sue for their share, even against another co-owner (D 9.2.19, 20).

### Non-owners with an analogous action (Obl. pp. 366–367)
- **Usufructuary** (USUSFRUCTUS = the right to use another's thing and take its fruits, preserving its substance, Paulus D 7.1.1, Prop. p. 181): Julian considers the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE, Ulpian prefers an ACTIO UTILIS (D 9.2.11.10). Paulus gives it even against the owner (D 9.2.12).
- **Pledgee** (right of pledge = the right to be satisfied from the proceeds of the thing, Prop. p. 189): up to the value of his secured claim; Paulus only if he has no other source of satisfaction (D 9.2.30.1).
- **BONA FIDE possessor** (wrongly believes he is the owner, Prop. p. 129): analogous action, even against the owner (D 9.2.11.8, D 9.2.17).
- Lessee or borrower liable for CUSTODIA: disputed; Julian says he needs no action (p. 367).

### FURTUM is not DAMNUM
FURTUM = taking another's movable with intent to enrich oneself, shown in an outward act (Obl. pp. 313–314; Prop. pp. 20–21). It gives the penal ACTIO FURTI and the reipersecutory CONDICTIO FURTIVA; between CONDICTIO FURTIVA and REI VINDICATIO the owner must choose (p. 315). DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM needs harm to the SUBSTANCE of the thing. Taking a thing away without intent to enrich oneself and without destroying it is neither: the jurists give an ACTIO IN FACTUM, e.g. for freeing a boar from a hunter's trap (Proculus D 41.1.55, Obl. p. 338).

### Possession and self-help
Possession is a fact, protected by interdicts; ownership is decided by the REI VINDICATIO (Prop. p. 68). Self-help is the exception: VIM VI REPELLERE LICET, you may retake by force from someone who took the thing from you by force (Prop. p. 18). Otherwise it can be unlawful: Proculus holds liable a man who tore down his neighbour's overhanging canopy instead of suing (D 9.2.29.1, Obl. p. 350).

terms.def: The property right that gives the owner (DOMINUS) exclusive control over a thing; also PROPRIETAS (Prop. p. 68).
Taking another's movable property, without authorisation, with intent to enrich oneself, shown in an outward act (Obl. pp. 313–314).
'It is permitted to repel force with force': one of the few cases of permitted self-help in Roman law (Prop. p. 18).

cards.q: Who is primarily entitled to bring the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE?
cards.a:
The OWNER (DOMINUS) of the harmed thing: the statute says DOMINO DARE (Ulpian D 9.2.11.6).
• Co-owners: each for his share, even against another co-owner
• For a slave: the master's financial loss counts, not the slave's pain

cards.q: Which non-owners get an analogous action for damage to a thing?
cards.a:
Usufructuary (and usuary), pledgee and BONA FIDE possessor.
• Pledgee: up to his secured claim (Paulus: only if he has no other satisfaction)
• Usufructuary and bona fide possessor: even against the owner
• Lessee/borrower with CUSTODIA liability: disputed (Julian: no)

cards.q: FURTUM vs DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM — what is the difference?
cards.a:
FURTUM = taking another's movable with intent to enrich oneself (DOLUS); DAMNUM = destroying or damaging its substance (DOLUS or CULPA).
• Taking away without enrichment intent and without destruction: neither → ACTIO IN FACTUM
• Theft and then killing a slave: ACTIO FURTI and ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE (D 9.2.27 pr)

cards.q: Proculus D 41.1.55: someone frees a boar from a hunter's trap. Liability?
cards.a:
No ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE (the boar is not harmed); Proculus favours an ACTIO IN FACTUM for the hunter's loss of his property.
• The hunter had acquired possession and ownership by OCCUPATIO
• No FURTUM: no intent to enrich oneself

cards.q: When does Roman law permit self-help?
cards.a:
Only exceptionally: VIM VI REPELLERE LICET — you may retake by force from someone who possesses VI towards you (Prop. p. 18).
• Removing a water pipe laid through your house without permission: permitted self-help (D 9.2.29.1)
• Tearing down a neighbour's overhanging canopy yourself: liable, you should have sued (Proculus)

3.title: Direct or indirect harm: which action?
3.text:
Roman jurists use a **graded concept** (Obl. p. 330). Only harm inflicted ACTIVELY and DIRECTLY falls under the statute itself → **ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE** (the ACTIO DIRECTA). Harm caused INDIRECTLY or by OMISSION gets a praetorian remedy modelled on it → **ACTIO UTILIS** or **ACTIO IN FACTUM** (p. 316). The test: did he cause the loss 'with his own body', CORPORE SUO DAMNUM DEDERIT (Gai. 3.219)? Analogous actions, too, require unlawfulness and fault (p. 340).

### Chapter 1: slaves and PECUDES
PECUDES = four-legged herd animals: sheep, goats, cattle, mules, donkeys, also working elephants and camels; pigs disputed (Labeo: yes); dogs and wild animals are not PECUDES (Gaius D 9.2.2.2, p. 327). Killing a dog or a goose falls under chapter 3 (p. 316).

| | OCCIDERE | MORTIS CAUSAM PRAESTARE |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | active, immediate killing with one's own body | 'providing a cause of death' by omission or an indirect act |
| Action | ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE | ACTIO IN FACTUM / UTILIS |
| Examples | hands, heel, sword, cudgel, projectile; throwing down a load (D 9.2.7.2); a faulty operation (D 9.2.7.8) | starving a slave one must feed (D 9.2.9.2); handing over poison that the slave drinks himself (D 9.2.7.6); luring a slave into a trap where another kills him (D 9.2.9.3); driving oxen over a ridge (Neratius D 9.2.53) |

Force (VIS) is not required (p. 331). Pushing a slave off a bridge is OCCIDERE even if he drowns later (Celsus in D 9.2.7.7, Case 263). If N pushes O onto Q's slave, Q has only an ACTIO IN FACTUM against N; O is not liable (Proculus in D 9.2.7.3). A provoked dog bites a slave: Proculus gives the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE; Julian only if the provoker held the dog, otherwise an ACTIO IN FACTUM (D 9.2.11.5).

### Chapter 3: everything else
- **URERE** (burning): a torch thrust into a slave's face; setting fire to a house, with liability for each neighbouring house that catches fire (D 9.2.27.6–8). Straw burnt on one's own field spreads to the neighbour's field: majority ACTIO IN FACTUM (Coll 12.7.4–5, Case 265).
- **FRANGERE** (breaking): a glass cup, a door, a building, a bone (D 9.2.27.29, 31).
- **RUMPERE** (wounding), widened to **CORRUMPERE**: any damage to property not under chapter 1, e.g. soiling clothes, pouring grain into a river, spilling wine, mixing sand into grain (D 9.2.27.15–20).
- **Consuming** another's wine or grain without permission → ACTIO UTILIS (Paulus D 9.2.30.2, Case 269).

terms.def: Active, immediate killing of a chapter-1 object with one's own body (CORPORE SUO); gives the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE (Obl. p. 330).
'Providing a cause of death': killing by omission or indirect action; gives an ACTIO IN FACTUM or ACTIO UTILIS (Obl. p. 331).
Praetorian actions modelled on the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE for harm caused indirectly or by omission (Obl. pp. 316, 330).

cards.q: ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE (directa) vs ACTIO UTILIS / IN FACTUM — when which?
cards.a:
The ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE only for active, direct harm 'with one's own body' (CORPORE SUO, Gai. 3.219); harm caused indirectly or by omission → ACTIO UTILIS or IN FACTUM.
• Analogous actions still require unlawfulness and fault
• Also called ACTIO AD EXEMPLUM LEGIS AQUILIAE

cards.q: OCCIDERE vs MORTIS CAUSAM PRAESTARE — what is the difference?
cards.a:
OCCIDERE = active, immediate killing with one's own body → ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE; MORTIS CAUSAM PRAESTARE = providing a cause of death by omission or an indirect act → ACTIO IN FACTUM / UTILIS.
• Force (VIS) is not required for OCCIDERE

cards.q: Which animals are PECUDES under chapter 1?
cards.a:
Four-legged herd animals: sheep, goats, cattle, mules, donkeys, also working elephants and camels (Gaius D 9.2.2.2).
• Pigs disputed (Labeo: yes)
• Dogs and wild animals: no → killing them falls under chapter 3

cards.q: Celsus (D 9.2.7.7): a slave is pushed off a bridge and drowns after struggling in the water. Which action?
cards.a:
The ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE (OCCIDERE) in every variant: died of the push, went under at once, or drowned later.
• The push actively and directly set the chain in motion
• Same for hurling a slave against a rock: direct physical contact

cards.q: What does CORRUMPERE mean in chapter 3?
cards.a:
The jurists' wide reading of RUMPERE: any destruction of or damage to property not covered by chapter 1.
• e.g. soiling clothes, pouring grain into a river, spilling wine, mixing sand into grain
• Covers inanimate things and animals that are not PECUDES (dog, goose)

cards.q: Ulpian D 9.2.11.5: T provokes a dog, which bites U's slave. What do Proculus and Julian say?
cards.a:
Proculus: ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE without distinction; Julian: only if T was holding the dog, otherwise ACTIO IN FACTUM.
• Explanation: only a dog held by T is his direct instrument
• A controversy on the line between direct and indirect harm

4.title: The four-stage scheme
4.text:
Benke/Meissel (Obl. pp. 327–329): the Roman jurists already separated these four stages, and they are still the basic test for delictual liability. In an exegesis they are the skeleton of your DOGMATIC EXPLANATION: say at which stage the jurist decides.

| Stage | Question | Roman terms | Typical fragments |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Statutory definition (with causation) | Chapter 1 (OCCIDERE a slave or PECUS) or chapter 3 (URERE, FRANGERE, (COR)RUMPERE)? Direct → ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE; indirect or omission → ACTIO UTILIS / IN FACTUM. Did the conduct cause the loss? | OCCIDERE, MORTIS CAUSAM PRAESTARE, CORPORE SUO | midwife D 9.2.9 pr; bridge D 9.2.7.7 |
| 2. Unlawfulness (INIURIA, objective) | Fulfilling the definition INDICATES unlawfulness. Is there a justification? | self-defence, necessity, self-help, authorisation, consent | lantern D 9.2.52.1; nets D 9.2.29.3 |
| 3. Culpability (INIURIA, subjective) | DOLUS or CULPA? A ground excluding fault? The victim's own carelessness? | DOLUS, CULPA, DILIGENTIA, CASUS | pruner D 9.2.31; barber D 9.2.11 pr; javelin D 9.2.9.4 |
| 4. Amount | Ch. 1: highest value in the past YEAR; ch. 3: within the next 30 DAYS; the victim's interest by the difference method | DAMNUM EMERGENS, LUCRUM CESSANS | D 9.2.22.1; D 9.2.33 pr |

### Causation (Obl. pp. 340–343)
- **CONDICIO SINE QUA NON**: think the act away (for an omission, think the correct conduct in); if the harm disappears, the conduct was causal. All such conditions count equally.
- **Adequacy** (modern): the cause must not be wholly untypical. The Romans did not distinguish this explicitly; the typified acts of the statute already imply causation. Labeo: lightly pushing a sickly slave who dies is enough (D 9.2.7.5). But if a slave dies of a non-fatal wound because his master neglects treatment, the injurer is liable only for wounding (VULNERARE = RUMPERE), not killing (Paulus D 9.2.30.4).
- **Overtaking causation**: both injurers are liable (D 9.2.51; D 9.2.11.3). **Alternative and cumulative causation**: each is liable in full, justified by the penal character (D 9.2.11.2, 11.4).

### Amount (pp. 360–363)
The victim is put where he would be without the harm. The 'year' is disputed: Celsus counts back from the death, Julian and the prevailing view from the mortal blow (D 9.2.21.1; D 9.2.51.2). Recoverable: medical costs; the fall in value of a group, e.g. a troupe or quadriga (Paulus D 9.2.22.1, Case 277). LUCRUM CESSANS only if realistic: cut nets, not the lost catch (D 9.2.29.3). No sentimental value (Paulus D 9.2.33 pr, Case 278).

terms.def: An indispensable condition: the conduct cannot be thought away without the harm disappearing; all such conditions count as equivalent (Obl. p. 340).
Actual loss in value of the assets / lost profit; lost profit is compensated only if it was realistic, not speculative (Obl. pp. 319, 361–362).

cards.q: What are the four stages of liability under the LEX AQUILIA?
cards.a:
1. statutory definition (incl. causation) → 2. unlawfulness (INIURIA, objective) → 3. culpability (INIURIA, subjective) → 4. amount.
• Stage 1 also decides ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE vs analogous action
• If stage 2 fails (justification), fault is not examined

cards.q: What does 'the statutory definition indicates unlawfulness' mean?
cards.a:
Conduct falling under chapter 1 or 3 (or an analogous case) is presumed unlawful, because it harms another's property.
• The presumption is rebutted only by a justification
• Textual basis: the statute ties the sanction to INIURIA OCCIDERE

cards.q: How do you test CONDICIO SINE QUA NON for an act and for an omission?
cards.a:
Act: think it away — if the harm disappears, it was causal. Omission: think the correct conduct in — if the harm disappears, the omission was causal.
• All such conditions count equally (equivalence)

cards.q: Paulus D 9.2.30.4: A gives B's slave a non-fatal wound; the slave dies because B neglects his treatment. Liability?
cards.a:
A is liable only for wounding (VULNERARE = RUMPERE, chapter 3), not for killing.
• The wound is causal for the death but presumably not its adequate cause
• A does not answer for the master's neglect of his slave

cards.q: How is the amount calculated under chapter 1 and chapter 3?
cards.a:
Chapter 1: the HIGHEST value in the year before; chapter 3: what the matter comes to within the next 30 days.
• 'Year' disputed: Celsus from the death, Julian/prevailing view from the mortal blow
• PLURIMI ('highest') is read into chapter 3 by interpretation (D 9.2.29.8)

cards.q: What does compensation of the victim's 'interest' include, and what not?
cards.a:
DAMNUM EMERGENS plus realistic LUCRUM CESSANS, calculated by the difference method.
• Yes: medical costs; fall in value of a group (band, troupe, quadriga, D 9.2.22.1)
• No: sentimental value (Paulus D 9.2.33 pr); speculative gains (lost catch)

5.title: Unlawfulness, fault and the victim's own carelessness
5.text:
### Stage 2: justifications (Obl. pp. 344–352)
Fulfilling the statutory definition indicates unlawfulness. A justification makes the act lawful: no liability, and fault is no longer examined (p. 345).
- **Self-defence**: against a PRESENT, UNLAWFUL attack on life, body or property; proportionate, no more harm than necessary; harm to a third party is not justified. Killing a slave who ambushes you to rob you: not liable (Gaius D 9.2.4 pr, Case 270). Putative self-defence does not justify, but may exclude fault.
- **Necessity**: harming a third party to save one's own interest from a danger one did not culpably create; last resort; suitable. A blameless crew cuts nets in a storm: justified (D 9.2.29.3, Case 272). Pulling down a neighbour's house against a fire: Celsus justifies it even if the fire never arrives, if done IUSTO METU, from reasonable fear (D 9.2.49.1); Servius is stricter.
- **Permitted self-help**, **authorisation** of magistrates, **consent** (glass cutters, D 9.2.27.29).

### Stage 3: fault (pp. 352–355)
CULPA in the broad sense has two degrees: **DOLUS** (the harm is foreseen and accepted) and **CULPA** in the narrow sense (negligence: failing to show due care, DILIGENTIA). Even the slightest negligence, CULPA LEVISSIMA, suffices (D 9.2.44 pr). The standard is objective: the VIR BONUS or BONUS PATER FAMILIAS, adapted to the activity (the 'good doctor', the 'good barber'). Harm that could not be foreseen is chance, CASUS: a ball player who pushes a slave boy who breaks his leg is not liable (Alfenus D 9.2.52.4).
No fault: the FURIOSUS and the INFANS (up to 7); older children are assessed individually (D 9.2.5.2); a person acting on his DOMINUS' or PATER FAMILIAS' order.

### The victim's own carelessness (pp. 356–358)
Roman law does NOT divide the loss: the injurer pays everything or nothing. Modern explanations: **culpa compensation** (the victim's carelessness outweighs the injurer's CULPA, never his DOLUS) and **acting at one's own risk** (entering a typically dangerous situation).
- **Barber** (Ulpian, Mela, Proculus D 9.2.11 pr): a ball strikes a barber's hand and the razor cuts the throat of the slave being shaved. Shaving where ball is played is negligent, but Proculus: whoever lets himself be shaved in a dangerous place has himself to blame.
- **Javelin** (Ulpian D 9.2.9.4): throwing for fun and killing a slave → CULPA, liable; on a practice field → not liable; aiming at the slave on purpose → DOLUS, liable.

terms.def: The two degrees of fault: DOLUS = the harmful result is foreseen and accepted; CULPA = negligence, failing to show due care (DILIGENTIA). CULPA also means fault in general (Obl. pp. 352–353).
Chance: injury that was unforeseeable or unavoidable; no fault and so no liability (Obl. p. 329).
'From reasonable fear': Celsus justifies demolishing a neighbour's house against a fire that never arrives if the demolisher acted from reasonable fear (D 9.2.49.1, Obl. p. 349).

cards.q: What are the requirements of self-defence?
cards.a:
A present, unlawful attack on a protected interest (life, body, property), repelled proportionately and with no more harm than necessary.
• No self-defence once the attack is over
• Harm to a third party is not justified
• Attacker need not be at fault (e.g. a FURIOSUS)

cards.q: When does necessity justify harm, and how is the ship-and-nets case decided (D 9.2.29.3)?
cards.a:
Harm to a third party to save one's own interest from a danger one did not culpably create, as a suitable last resort.
• Blameless crew cuts nets/anchor lines → justified
• Crew partly to blame → no necessity; liable if culpable — for the nets, not the lost catch

cards.q: DOLUS vs CULPA — what is the difference?
cards.a:
DOLUS: the actor foresees and accepts the harm; CULPA (narrow sense): no intent, but he fails to show due care although he could and should have foreseen the harm.
• CULPA also means fault in general
• Even CULPA LEVISSIMA suffices (D 9.2.44 pr)

cards.q: By which standard is negligence measured under the LEX AQUILIA?
cards.a:
An objective standard (CULPA IN ABSTRACTO): the VIR BONUS / BONUS PATER FAMILIAS.
• Adapted to the activity: 'good doctor' (BONUS MEDICUS), 'good barber' (BONUS TONSOR)
• Meeting the standard = no liability even if harm follows

cards.q: How does Roman law treat the victim's own carelessness?
cards.a:
It does not split the loss: the injurer is liable for everything or for nothing.
• Culpa compensation: the victim's carelessness outweighs the injurer's CULPA (never DOLUS)
• Acting at one's own risk: entering a typically dangerous situation

cards.q: Barber's case (D 9.2.11 pr): a ball hits the barber's hand and the razor cuts the slave's throat. What does Proculus say?
cards.a:
Shaving where ball is played is negligent, but whoever lets himself be shaved in a dangerous place has himself to blame.
• Barber presumably not liable if the slave could see the risk
• Mela: whoever was at fault is liable (the ball player is left open)

cards.q: Javelin case (D 9.2.9.4): when is the javelin thrower liable for killing a slave?
cards.a:
Throwing for fun → CULPA, liable; on a field set aside for practice → not liable; aiming at the slave on purpose → DOLUS, liable.
• Practice field explained by: acting at one's own risk, culpa compensation, or a different standard of care

6.title: Mini exegesis 1: D 9.2.9 pr (the midwife)
6.text:
Benke/Meissel Case 264 (Obl. pp. 331–332). A classic for stage 1: OCCIDERE or MORTIS CAUSAM PRAESTARE?

### Text (summary after Benke/Meissel; read the full translation in Watson, D 9.2.9 pr)
ULPIAN, reporting LABEO: a midwife gave a medicine to a woman (from the context, a slave), who died. Labeo distinguishes: if the midwife put the medicine into her mouth with her own hands, she killed; if she only handed it over and the woman took it herself, an ACTIO IN FACTUM is given.

### BASIC PART
1. Facts: Midwife M gives a medicine to O's slave woman S, who dies of it. Variant 1: M puts it into S's mouth herself. Variant 2: M hands it over and S takes it herself.
2. Legal question: Is M liable to O for S's death, and with which action?
3. Decision: The author is ULPIAN; he reports LABEO's distinction and does not contradict it, so there is one opinion. V1: OCCIDERE → ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE. V2: no OCCIDERE but MORTIS CAUSAM PRAESTARE → ACTIO IN FACTUM.

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. Institution: DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM, chapter 1 (killing another's slave).
5. Claim: O v M for compensation of the value of S. Basis: M caused the death of O's slave; the statute pays the DOMINUS.
6. Remedies: V1 ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE (ACTIO DIRECTA); V2 ACTIO IN FACTUM modelled on it. Amount: the highest value of S in the past year.

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. Similar cases: poison given instead of medicine and swallowed by the slave → ACTIO IN FACTUM; a sword handed to a mentally ill slave → ACTIO IN FACTUM (Celsus in D 9.2.7.6, Case 263); a faulty operation is OCCIDERE (D 9.2.7.8).
8. Controversies: none in the text. In a parallel (the provoked dog, D 9.2.11.5) Proculus and Julian disagree on the same line.
9. Dogmatic explanation: The text decides stage 1. The ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE needs harm caused CORPORE SUO (Gai. 3.219). In V1 M's own hands bring the medicine into the body. In V2 the slave's own act stands between M's conduct and the death, so M only 'provides a cause of death'. The question is not WHETHER M can be liable but WITH WHICH ACTION: the statute covers the obvious core cases, the praetorian analogy the rest (p. 330). The text does not discuss unlawfulness and fault; say that both remain necessary for either action (p. 340).

terms.def: Causing loss 'with one's own body': the test for direct harm under the LEX AQUILIA (Gai. 3.219, Obl. p. 330).

cards.q: D 9.2.9 pr (midwife) — What are the facts and the legal question?
cards.a:
A midwife gives a medicine to a slave woman, who dies; V1 she puts it into her mouth, V2 she hands it over and the slave takes it herself.
• Question: is the midwife liable to the owner, and with which action?

cards.q: D 9.2.9 pr (midwife) — What does Labeo decide?
cards.a:
V1 (into the mouth with her own hands) = OCCIDERE → ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE; V2 (handed over) = MORTIS CAUSAM PRAESTARE → ACTIO IN FACTUM.
• Author Ulpian reports Labeo's view; one opinion

cards.q: D 9.2.9 pr (midwife) — Why does the action change between the variants?
cards.a:
Only harm caused CORPORE SUO falls under the statute; when the slave takes the medicine herself, her own act stands between the midwife's conduct and the death.
• The difference concerns the ACTION, not WHETHER the midwife can be liable
• Parallel: poison handed over and swallowed → ACTIO IN FACTUM (D 9.2.7.6)

7.title: Mini exegesis 2: D 9.2.31 (the tree pruner)
7.text:
Benke/Meissel Case 274 (Obl. p. 354). A classic for stage 3: CULPA and its objective standard.

### Text (summary after Benke/Meissel; read the full translation in Watson, D 9.2.31)
PAULUS, reporting QUINTUS MUCIUS: a tree pruner dropped a cut branch, which killed a passing slave. Mucius: he is negligent if a path ran beneath the tree and he did not shout a timely warning. Paulus: if there was no path, there is no negligence; but if the pruner saw someone below and still dropped the branch, that is DOLUS.

### BASIC PART
1. Facts: Pruner P cuts branches; one falls and kills O's slave S, passing below. V1: a path runs under the tree and P gives no timely warning. V2: no path; S walks across open fields. V3: P sees S below and drops the branch anyway.
2. Legal question: Is P liable to O for S's death, i.e. was he at fault?
3. Decision: The author is PAULUS. He cites QUINTUS MUCIUS (a Republican jurist) for V1 and adds V2 and V3 himself. V1: CULPA → liable. V2: not foreseeable → no CULPA, not liable. V3: DOLUS → liable.

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. Institutions: DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM, chapter 1; fault in its two degrees, DOLUS and CULPA.
5. Claim: O v P for the value of the killed slave. Basis: P killed him unlawfully and culpably.
6. Remedy: the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE; the book lists killing by throwing down a load as OCCIDERE (Ulpian D 9.2.7.2, p. 330). Amount: the highest value in the past year.

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. Similar cases: Paulus D 9.2.28 pr–1 (fn 70); the ball game (Alfenus D 9.2.52.4): even a careful player need not play so as never to injure anyone → CASUS; the javelin thrower (D 9.2.9.4).
8. Controversies: none. Paulus agrees with Mucius and varies the facts.
9. Dogmatic explanation: Stages 1 and 2 are not in doubt; the text decides stage 3. CULPA means failing to take due care (DILIGENTIA), measured objectively: what a diligent person in P's place could and should have foreseen (VIR BONUS, p. 353). Where people pass, the deadly risk is foreseeable and a warning shout is the required care. On open fields nobody is to be expected, so the death is CASUS. If P sees S and drops the branch anyway, he foresees and accepts the harm: DOLUS. Paulus does not discuss the slave's own carelessness.

terms.def: Due care; whoever observes it acts correctly and is not liable even if harm follows (Obl. p. 353).

cards.q: D 9.2.31 (tree pruner) — What are the facts and the legal question?
cards.a:
A pruner drops a cut branch which kills a passing slave; variants: path below / no path / he sees someone and drops it anyway.
• Question: is the pruner liable to the slave's owner, i.e. was he at fault?

cards.q: D 9.2.31 (tree pruner) — How do Quintus Mucius and Paulus decide?
cards.a:
Mucius: path below and no timely warning → CULPA, liable. Paulus: no path (open fields) → not foreseeable, no CULPA, not liable.
• Paulus: if he saw someone below and still dropped it → DOLUS, liable
• No controversy: Paulus varies the facts

cards.q: D 9.2.31 (tree pruner) — Which stage of the scheme does the text decide, and by which standard?
cards.a:
Stage 3, culpability: could and should a diligent person have foreseen the danger?
• Objective standard (VIR BONUS); the place matters
• Parallel: the careful ball player is not liable, CASUS (Alfenus D 9.2.52.4)

8.title: Mini exegesis 3: D 9.2.52.1 (the innkeeper's lantern)
8.text:
Benke/Meissel Case 271 (Obl. pp. 346–348). A classic for stage 2: self-defence and its limits.

### Text (summary after Benke/Meissel; read the full translation in Watson, D 9.2.52.1)
ALFENUS: a passer-by carried off an innkeeper's lantern from the street; the innkeeper pursued him and in the fight knocked out one of his eyes. The decision depends on who attacked first and whether it was done on purpose.

### BASIC PART
1. Facts: Innkeeper K's lantern stands on the street; passer-by P takes it; K pursues him. V1: K holds P and demands the lantern; P strikes at K with a kind of lance to break free; in the brawl K knocks out P's eye. V2: as V1, but K has already overpowered P and then knocks out his eye on purpose. V3: K runs after P and starts hitting him; in the brawl he knocks out P's eye.
2. Legal question: Is K liable for the eye, or is the injury justified by self-defence?
3. Decision: The author is ALFENUS, a Republican jurist; nobody else is cited. V1: justified, not liable. V2: liable. V3: liable.

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. Institutions: DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM, chapter 3 (wounding); justification by self-defence.
5. Claim: compensation for P's injury against K. The text, as summarised, does not say whether P is free or a slave: for a slave, his owner sues (p. 365); the body of a free man cannot be valued in money (Gaius D 9.1.3, p. 321).
6. Remedy: the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE (a direct blow).

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. Similar cases: killing a slave who ambushes you to rob you is justified (Gaius D 9.2.4 pr, Case 270); harm to a third party in self-defence is not (Paulus D 9.2.45.4). The Twelve Tables let anyone kill an armed or nocturnal thief; Alfenus does not even consider it (p. 348).
8. Controversies: none in the text.
9. Dogmatic explanation: Stage 1 is fulfilled, so unlawfulness is indicated; the text decides stage 2. Self-defence needs a PRESENT, UNLAWFUL attack, a proportionate defence and no more harm than necessary (pp. 345–346). V1: P attacks K's body with a weapon: justified. V2: once P is overpowered the attack is over; K counter-attacks, an excess, and his intent shows fault. V3: only K's property was attacked; a cheap lantern cannot justify an eye, so this is excessive and K acted at least negligently. Self-defence protects; it does not punish.

terms.def: Defence that is disproportionate or continues after the attack is over; it is unlawful (Obl. pp. 346–347).

cards.q: D 9.2.52.1 (lantern) — What are the facts and the legal question?
cards.a:
A passer-by takes an innkeeper's lantern from the street; the innkeeper pursues him and in the fight knocks out his eye (three variants).
• Question: is the innkeeper liable, or is he justified by self-defence?

cards.q: D 9.2.52.1 (lantern) — How does Alfenus decide the three variants?
cards.a:
V1 (passer-by strikes first with a weapon) → self-defence, not liable; V2 (eye knocked out on purpose after overpowering him) → liable; V3 (innkeeper hits first) → liable.
• V2: attack over = excess, intent
• V3: only property attacked, a cheap lantern does not justify an eye

cards.q: D 9.2.52.1 (lantern) — Which stage does the text decide, and which rule explains it?
cards.a:
Stage 2, unlawfulness: self-defence justifies only against a present, unlawful attack, proportionately and with no more harm than necessary.
• Parallel: killing a slave who ambushes you to rob you is justified (D 9.2.4 pr)

9.title: Exegesis checklist: a Lex Aquilia fragment
9.text:
Use this when the exam fragment comes from Digest title 9.2 (AD LEGEM AQUILIAM) or a parallel.

| Item | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Facts | What was harmed: slave, PECUS, other animal, object? Who OWNS it? How did the harm happen: with the injurer's own body, indirectly, by omission? Was the injurer a slave or son in power? |
| Legal question | Usually: is X liable to the owner, under which chapter, with which action? Variants typically change one element (path / no path). |
| Decision | Author from the INSCRIPTIO; cited jurists (Labeo, Q. Mucius, Celsus, Proculus, Julian). Opinions often differ only on the ACTION. |
| Institution | DAMNUM INIURIA DATUM, chapter 1 or 3; define it in 1–2 sentences. |
| Claims | Owner v injurer. Usufructuary, pledgee, bona fide possessor by analogy. Against the holder of power if a slave or son acted. |
| Remedies | ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE / ACTIO UTILIS / ACTIO IN FACTUM; double if the defendant denies (Gai. 4.9). |
| Amount | Ch. 1: highest value in the past year; ch. 3: within 30 days; DAMNUM EMERGENS and realistic LUCRUM CESSANS; no sentimental value. |
| Concurrence | Contract and delict: in principle choose; Paulus lets the lender (COMMODATUM) claim the excess (D 44.7.34.2). After REI VINDICATIO the LA action must be given up (D 6.1.13). Theft and then killing: ACTIO FURTI and ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE (D 9.2.27 pr). |
| Similar cases | midwife ↔ poison (D 9.2.7.6); pruner ↔ ball game (D 9.2.52.4) ↔ javelin (D 9.2.9.4). |
| Controversies | Proculus v Julian (dog, D 9.2.11.5); Celsus v Julian (the 'year'); Q. Mucius v Pomponius (mare driven off, D 9.2.39); Celsus v Servius (house pulled down against fire); majority v minority (straw fire). |
| Dogmatic | Run the four stages and say which one the jurist decides; then the interests: protection of property against freedom of action. |

### Noxal liability (Obl. pp. 368–369)
If a slave (or person in power) did the harm: first test the PERPETRATOR's liability through all four stages. Then sue whoever holds power when the action is brought (NOXA CAPUT SEQUITUR); he can pay or surrender the perpetrator (NOXAE DEDITIO). If he knew and could have prevented it, or ordered it, he is liable directly as if he had acted himself, without NOXAE DEDITIO. The tenant whose slave let the villa burn (D 9.2.27.9) is also liable EX CONTRACTU for CULPA IN ELIGENDO (p. 335). Liability does not pass to the injurer's heirs, except for his enrichment (D 9.2.23.8).

terms.def: Noxal surrender: the holder of power discharges noxal liability by handing over the slave or son who did the harm, instead of paying (Obl. p. 368).
Noxal liability follows the person: decisive is who holds power over the perpetrator when the action is brought, not at the time of the deed (Obl. p. 368).

cards.q: How does noxal liability work under the LEX AQUILIA?
cards.a:
First test the perpetrator's (slave's) liability; then sue whoever holds power over him when the action is brought (NOXA CAPUT SEQUITUR), who may pay or surrender him (NOXAE DEDITIO).
• No surrender if the master knew and could have prevented it, or ordered it: direct liability

cards.q: Can the ACTIO LEGIS AQUILIAE be combined with a contractual action, the REI VINDICATIO or the ACTIO FURTI?
cards.a:
Contract: in principle the victim must choose (Paulus: the excess may still be claimed). REI VINDICATIO: the LA action must be given up. FURTUM: both actions (theft and then killing a slave).
• D 44.7.34.2; D 6.1.13; D 9.2.27 pr

10.title: Suretyship: FIDEIUSSIO, accessoriness and recourse
10.text:
### The problem (Obl. pp. 271–272)
A creditor wants protection against the debtor not paying: REAL security (a pledge on a thing) or PERSONAL security, a further person, the SURETY, liable with all his assets. Example 81: Agamemnon lends Nike 10,000 only after Pelias promises to pay if she cannot; Nike becomes insolvent, so Agamemnon claims from Pelias.
- Suretyship is a contract between CREDITOR and SURETY, tied to the main debt: a three-person relationship.
- Surety and debtor stand in an INTERNAL relationship, usually a MANDATE or NEGOTIORUM GESTIO.
- The creditor's right against the surety is only IN PERSONAM: if the surety is insolvent, he gets only a quota. A pledgee instead has priority in the pledged thing.
- SC VELLEIANUM: a woman's INTERCESSIO is valid, but she has the EXCEPTIO SC VELLEIANI.

### FIDEIUSSIO (pp. 273–274)
The most important classical form (the older SPONSIO and FIDEPROMISSIO could secure only stipulated debts). It is a STIPULATIO: the creditor asks 'QUOD MAEVIUS MIHI DEBET, ID FIDE TUA ESSE IUBES?', the surety answers yes. The creditor presumably sues with the ACTIO EX STIPULATU.
- Classical law: the surety is an alternative debtor of equal rank; the creditor chooses whom to sue, but (procedural consumption) can sue only one.
- Justinian: BENEFICIUM EXCUSSIONIS. The surety may send the creditor to the debtor first; suretyship becomes subsidiary.

### Accessoriness (pp. 274–276)
The surety promises exactly what the debtor owes, so the existence, duration and amount of his debt depend on the main debt.
- Paulus D 46.1.56.2 (Case 51a): a loan made with a third party's coins creates no loan, but once the debtor spends them he must repay by CONDICTIO, and the surety is liable for that.
- The surety can raise the debtor's defences that concern the debt itself, even against the debtor's will: EXCEPTIO DOLI, QUOD METUS CAUSA, REI IUDICATAE, PACTI DE NON PETENDO, SC MACEDONIANI. Not personal ones, e.g. the BENEFICIUM COMPETENTIAE.
- A natural obligation (a slave's loan) can be secured.

### Recourse (pp. 276–280)
- **Mandate** (surety at the debtor's request or with his apparent approval): ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA.
- **NEGOTIORUM GESTIO** (paying with the intention of recovering): ACTIO NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM CONTRARIA. Surety against the debtor's express prohibition: disputed, most jurists refuse it.
- **Assignment**: the creditor transfers his claim to the paying surety, with its securities; under Justinian the surety has a right to this, the BENEFICIUM CEDENDARUM ACTIONUM.

terms.def: The main classical form of suretyship: a STIPULATIO in which the surety takes the debtor's debt 'upon his faith' (QUOD MAEVIUS MIHI DEBET, ID FIDE TUA ESSE IUBES?) (Obl. p. 273).
The surety's obligation depends on the principal debt for its existence, duration and amount, because he promises exactly what the debtor owes (Obl. p. 274).
Justinian's right of a paying surety to demand that the creditor assign him the claim against the principal debtor (Obl. p. 280).

cards.q: What is suretyship, and which persons are involved?
cards.a:
A further person (the surety) becomes personally liable with all his assets for the debtor's debt; a contract between creditor and surety, tied to the main debt.
• Three persons: creditor, principal debtor, surety
• Surety–debtor = the internal relationship (mandate or NEGOTIORUM GESTIO)

cards.q: Personal security (suretyship) vs real security (pledge) — what is the difference?
cards.a: Surety: liable with ALL his assets, but only IN PERSONAM — if he is insolvent the creditor gets a quota. Pledge: only the pledged thing, but a right in rem with priority, even in bankruptcy.

cards.q: How is a FIDEIUSSIO concluded?
cards.a:
As a STIPULATIO: the creditor asks 'QUOD MAEVIUS MIHI DEBET, ID FIDE TUA ESSE IUBES?' and the surety answers yes.
• Older forms SPONSIO and FIDEPROMISSIO secure only stipulated debts
• Creditor presumably sues with the ACTIO EX STIPULATU

cards.q: Classical law vs Justinian: is the FIDEIUSSOR liable equally or only subsidiarily?
cards.a: Classical: equal rank, an alternative debtor; the creditor chooses and, because of procedural consumption, can sue only one. Justinian: BENEFICIUM EXCUSSIONIS — the surety can send the creditor to the debtor first.

cards.q: What does the accessoriness of the FIDEIUSSIO mean?
cards.a:
The surety promises exactly what the debtor owes (QUOD MAEVIUS DEBET), so the existence, duration and amount of his debt depend on the main debt.
• Older SPONSIO/FIDEPROMISSIO follow the debtor's original promise instead

cards.q: Paulus D 46.1.56.2 (Case 51a): G lends D someone else's coins; B is FIDEIUSSOR. Is B liable?
cards.a:
Yes, once D spends the coins: D then owns them and must repay by CONDICTIO, and B answers for that.
• Handing over another's coins creates no MUTUUM, so at first nothing is owed
• B is surety for every legal ground arising from the transfer of the money

cards.q: Which of the debtor's defences can the surety raise against the creditor?
cards.a:
Those that concern the debt itself, even against the debtor's will: EXCEPTIO DOLI, QUOD METUS CAUSA, REI IUDICATAE, PACTI DE NON PETENDO, SC MACEDONIANI.
• Not personal ones: BENEFICIUM COMPETENTIAE (ID QUOD FACERE POTEST)
• A natural obligation (slave's loan) can be secured

cards.q: What is recourse, and on what does the surety's recourse depend?
cards.a:
The right of a secondary obligor to be reimbursed by the person to whom the debt materially belongs.
• It depends on the internal relationship between surety and debtor: usually mandate or NEGOTIORUM GESTIO

cards.q: A woman stands surety for another's debt. Is this valid?
cards.a:
Yes, but under the SC VELLEIANUM (which forbids women to intercede for others) she can defend herself against the creditor with the EXCEPTIO SC VELLEIANI.
• Standing surety is an INTERCESSIO: stepping between creditor and debtor

cards.q: Can a natural obligation, e.g. a slave's loan, be secured by suretyship?
cards.a:
Yes: the creditor may sue the surety although he has no enforceable claim against the slave.
• But a loan against the SC MACEDONIANUM: its EXCEPTIO concerns the debt itself, so the surety can raise it too

cards.q: By which routes can a paying surety take recourse against the debtor?
cards.a:
Mandate → ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA; NEGOTIORUM GESTIO → ACTIO NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM CONTRARIA; assignment of the creditor's claim (MANDATUM IN REM SUAM).
• Under Justinian: a right to assignment, BENEFICIUM CEDENDARUM ACTIONUM
• Assignment also brings the securities attached to the claim

cards.q: Does a surety who stood surety against the debtor's express prohibition have recourse?
cards.a:
Disputed: most jurists refuse the ACTIO NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM CONTRARIA (unwanted meddling deserves no protection).
• Some allow an action (at least an ACTIO UTILIS): the debtor is enriched by being freed
• Against recourse: Paulus and Pomponius (D 17.1.40)

cards.q: When does a surety acting as NEGOTIORUM GESTOR NOT get recourse against the debtor, and what can he do instead?
cards.a:
If he paid a debt that did not exist, or the debtor had a permanent EXCEPTIO against the creditor: the intervention was not useful.
• Instead: CONDICTIO INDEBITI against the creditor (Ulpian D 12.6.25, Case 51e)

11.title: Mini exegesis 4: D 17.1.29.3 (the surety who did not tell)
11.text:
Benke/Meissel Case 177 (Obl. pp. 277–278). A classic for recourse under a mandate; links to the class of 9 December (mandatum).

### Text (summary after Benke/Meissel; read the full translation in Watson, D 17.1.29.3)
ULPIAN: a surety acting on the debtor's mandate paid the creditor without informing the debtor; then the debtor paid as well. The surety sues the debtor with the ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA. Ulpian denies the claim, but the debtor must cede to the surety his own claim against the creditor.

### BASIC PART
1. Facts: D owes C money. On D's mandate G stands surety for this debt. G pays C without telling D. Later D, not knowing this, also pays C. G now wants his money back from D.
2. Legal question: Can G recover his payment from D, and if not, what can he do?
3. Decision: The author is ULPIAN; no other jurist is cited. G has no claim against D: failing to inform D comes very close to DOLUS. But G can require D to cede to him the CONDICTIO INDEBITI that D has against C.

### INTERPRETATIVE PART
4. Institutions: FIDEIUSSIO (relation C–G); MANDATUM (internal relation D–G); CONDICTIO INDEBITI (recovery of a payment that was not owed).
5. Claims: G v D, reimbursement as expenses of the mandate: denied. D v C, return of the second payment: after G's payment D was released and owed nothing. G v D: cession of that claim.
6. Remedies: ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA (denied); CONDICTIO INDEBITI, ceded to G.

### DOGMATIC EXPLANATION
7. Similar cases: a surety who pays a debt that did not exist, or where the debtor had a permanent EXCEPTIO, recovers from the creditor by CONDICTIO INDEBITI (Ulpian D 12.6.25, Case 51e); a paying surety, as it were, buys the creditor's claim (Paulus D 46.1.36, Case 51h).
8. Controversies: none in the text.
9. Dogmatic explanation: Recourse depends on the internal relationship (p. 277). Under a mandate the surety claims his payment as expenses of the mandate. But mandator and mandatarius owe each other further duties, here a duty to inform, so that the creditor is not paid twice. Ulpian treats the breach as CULPA LATA, for which even a mandatarius is liable (p. 278). Result: G carries the burden he created. He must get the second payment back from C himself and bears the risk of C's insolvency, while D, who paid in good faith, is protected.

terms.def: Action to recover what was paid in the mistaken belief that it was owed (Obl. pp. 278–279).
Gross negligence; Ulpian classifies the surety's failure to inform the debtor as CULPA LATA, for which even a mandatarius is liable (Obl. p. 278).

cards.q: D 17.1.29.3 — What are the facts and the legal question?
cards.a:
Surety G (on D's mandate) pays creditor C without telling D; then D also pays C. G sues D for reimbursement.
• Question: can G recover his payment from D, and if not, what can he do?

cards.q: D 17.1.29.3 — What does Ulpian decide?
cards.a:
G has no ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA against D: failing to inform D comes very close to DOLUS (CULPA LATA).
• But D must cede to G his CONDICTIO INDEBITI against C

cards.q: D 17.1.29.3 — Why does D have a CONDICTIO INDEBITI against C at all?
cards.a:
G's payment had already discharged the debt, so D's second payment paid a debt that was no longer owed.
• G must recover it from C himself and bears the risk of C's insolvency

12.title: Exegesis checklist: a suretyship fragment
12.text:
Use this when the exam fragment is about a FIDEIUSSOR (Digest title 46.1, or a mandate text in title 17.1).

| Item | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Facts | Name the persons: creditor C, principal debtor D, surety G (several: G1, G2 …). Who asked G to stand surety? Who paid whom, when, and was the other told? |
| Legal question | Usually one of three: Is G liable at all (accessoriness)? Can G use D's defence? Can G get his money back (recourse), and from whom? |
| Decision | Note whether the text reflects classical law (free choice of the creditor, consumption) or Justinian (BENEFICIUM EXCUSSIONIS, BENEFICIUM CEDENDARUM ACTIONUM). |
| Institution | FIDEIUSSIO (a STIPULATIO) plus the internal relation (MANDATUM or NEGOTIORUM GESTIO), often plus the secured contract (MUTUUM, sale). |
| Claims and remedies | C v G: ACTIO EX STIPULATU. G v D: ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA / NEGOTIORUM GESTORUM CONTRARIA / assigned claim. G v C: CONDICTIO INDEBITI. G v co-sureties: only with an assigned claim. |
| Defences | Defences concerning the debt itself: yes. Personal ones (BENEFICIUM COMPETENTIAE): no. A woman as surety: EXCEPTIO SC VELLEIANI. |
| Dogmatic | Accessoriness (G owes what D owes); who bears the risk of insolvency; the duties of the internal relation. |

### Several sureties (Obl. pp. 280–282)
Example 82: C lends D 120,000; W, X, Y and Z are sureties; D is insolvent.
- **LEX APULEIA** (SPONSIO, FIDEPROMISSIO): each is liable for the whole (joint liability, IN SOLIDUM), but the one who paid has pro-rata recourse: W pays 120,000 and claims 30,000 from each of X, Y and Z.
- **LEX FURIA DE SPONSU**: each is liable only for his share (several liability): C can claim only 30,000 from each and must sue each separately.
- **FIDEIUSSIO**: these statutes do not apply; originally each co-surety was liable in full. The **EPISTULA HADRIANI**: all SOLVENT co-sureties are liable proportionately, so they share the risk of insolvency: 30,000 each; if one is insolvent, the other three owe 40,000 each. **BENEFICIUM DIVISIONIS**: a co-surety can require the creditor to divide the claim, but must prove the others solvent (Paulus D 46.1.28, Case 51c). A co-surety who pays everything without invoking it has recourse against the others only if the creditor's claim was assigned to him (Modestinus D 46.1.39, Case 51d).

terms.def: Hadrian's rescript for co-FIDEIUSSORES: all solvent co-sureties are liable proportionately; it also gives the BENEFICIUM DIVISIONIS (Obl. p. 282).
Joint: each debtor owes the whole (IN SOLIDUM), but the creditor receives it only once; several: each owes only a proportionate part (Obl. p. 281).

cards.q: LEX APULEIA vs LEX FURIA DE SPONSU — how do they treat co-sureties?
cards.a:
LEX APULEIA: each liable for the whole, with pro-rata recourse against the others; LEX FURIA: each liable only for his share.
• Both apply only to SPONSIO and FIDEPROMISSIO, not to FIDEIUSSIO

cards.q: What does the EPISTULA HADRIANI provide for co-FIDEIUSSORES?
cards.a:
All SOLVENT co-sureties are liable proportionately, so they share the risk that the debtor or a co-surety is insolvent.
• BENEFICIUM DIVISIONIS: a co-surety can demand that the claim be divided, proving the others solvent
• Who pays all without invoking it has recourse only with an assigned claim (D 46.1.39)

cards.q: Example 82: debt 120,000, four co-FIDEIUSSORES, the debtor insolvent. What does each owe under the EPISTULA HADRIANI — and if one surety is also insolvent?
cards.a: 30,000 each; if one co-surety is insolvent, the remaining three owe 40,000 each.
